headline: A CMP enrollment left waiting can be picked up by a later process instead of started again.
summary:
A certification authority that answers waiting can take hours to decide, and pki.cmp.session held the whole exchange in memory: its transaction identifier, its nonce chain, and the key it asked to have certified. When the poll budget ran out the session returned poll-timeout and that state was gone, so a caller whose process ended had no way to collect a certificate that was later issued for a request it had already made.

A poll-timeout now carries a resumeToken, and session.resumePoll(token) continues the same transaction. The token is plain JSON that survives a restart, it carries no secret, and it grants nothing: every response on the resumed poll is protection-verified and nonce-bound, and the grant is held to the key the token names, exactly as the first process did.

Added: A pki.cmp.session poll-timeout verdict carries resumeToken, and session.resumePoll(token) continues that transaction in a later process. The authority's polling interval is waited out before the first resumed request, while the resuming session's own maxTotalWait still bounds it: a remainder longer than that budget times out immediately and hands the same due time on. A further timeout returns another token, so a wait can span any number of processes, and the polls each one spent accumulate across them. Each timeout reports the waiting status, whether or not that process read a certificate response of its own, so a wait split across processes reads the same as one held in a single process. The authority's own statusString and failInfo are not reproduced from the token, so a verdict never presents text as the authority's that it did not send in that exchange. A session that has already run a transaction refuses to resume one, since RFC 9810 section 5.1.1 gives each transaction its own identifier.

The token is plain JSON, so it survives being written to disk and read back. It names the transaction identifier the exchange is keyed by, the nonce the next request must echo (RFC 9810 section 5.1.1), which request is being polled as a decimal string so an identifier of any width survives, the response arm its grant arrives on, whether the request that opened the transaction asked for implicit confirmation, the polls already spent, the public key the granted certificate must certify, the signer identity the first process authenticated and, separately, the certificate it currently verifies a response with when that response omits its extraCerts, the certificates the authority had already sent including any it delivered only on a waiting leg, and the instant its own checkAfter allows the next poll. It carries no secret, because the protection material, the trust anchors and the endpoint come from the session the caller builds to resume with.

A resumed poll grants nothing the first process would not have accepted. It protection-verifies and nonce-binds every response before reading it, holds every response to the signer identity the token names, refuses a granted certificate that certifies a different key, and confirms the grant with the same certConf handshake. Those fields are what the resumed session holds the exchange to, so a token is integrity-sensitive and belongs in storage the caller controls: someone who can rewrite it can widen what the resumed session accepts, up to the limit of that session's own trust anchors and the authority's protection, which a rewritten token cannot reach past. Store it where the enrollment's own state is stored, and read it back into a session configured the way the first one was. The token carries what the transaction established and the session supplies the rest, so the protection material, the trust anchors, the endpoint and a sender pinned with opts.expectedSender are all given again: a resumed poll accepts and refuses exactly what an uninterrupted one in the same session would, which means it also refuses a response that session has no way to authenticate.

A token that cannot carry the transaction is refused with cmp/bad-input before any request is sent, so stored state that cannot be used never spends the nonce the token is the only copy of. That covers a value that is not an object, one that names no transaction, a non-hex transaction identifier or non-canonical base64 nonce, a transaction identifier that is not the 128 bits a first message opens one with or a nonce shorter than the 128 bits a response must carry (RFC 9483 section 3.1 and 3.5), both of which name state no exchange could have produced, a request identifier written in any spelling other than the decimal one a session writes, a response arm that is not an enrollment arm, an unknown field, a key that is not a SubjectPublicKeyInfo, a field that names a certificate and is not one, and more certificates than the list it restores can hold. The two fields that bind the transaction are required rather than optional, since a token lives in storage where it can be edited and dropping a field must not drop the check it feeds: the key the grant is held to, and, for a signature session, the identity every response is held to. A shared-secret session pins no certificate, and its secret is the binding instead. The token also names how the transaction authenticates, and a session that authenticates the other way is refused: a signature transaction is bound by the pinned signer identity and a shared-secret one by the secret, so neither resumes the other's. How the grant is confirmed comes from the token rather than from the resuming session's own opts.implicitConfirm, since it was negotiated in the request the token continues: a session that never set the option still confirms an implicitly confirmed grant without a certConf, and one that sets it cannot make a transaction whose request never asked for it accept an implicit-confirm indication. A token that omits the field resumes as though the request asked for nothing. A token that asked for it is refused by a session carrying opts.acceptCert, the same pairing the constructor refuses, since an implicitly confirmed grant leaves no certConf leg for a policy to reject on.
Changed: pki.cmp.session refuses an opts.maxResponseBytes that is not a whole number of bytes between 1 and the 24 MiB transport ceiling, at construction, with cmp/bad-input. It is the bound the response reads and the restored certificate pools are measured against, and pki.acme.client already held the option to the same range. A session that passed a fractional or out-of-range value previously carried it as far as the first read.
